claims.text: The as-deposited protective coating has a dual-phase microstructure containing distinct FCC and BCC regions.
The coating's creep resistance is governed by a synergistic effect of FCC/BCC interphase boundaries.
Misfit and local lattice distortions occur at the FCC/BCC interfaces.
Misfit and local lattice distortions at FCC/BCC interfaces impede dislocation glide and climb during continuous loading.
Changing deposition temperature or cooling rate can systematically vary the relative fractions of the FCC and BCC phases.
Varying the FCC/BCC phase fractions can produce coatings with different or optimized interphase-boundary densities.
FCC/BCC interphase boundaries generate local misfit strain and high lattice friction.
FCC/BCC interphase boundaries serve as obstacles to dislocation motion.
Crystallographic mismatch and local compositional fluctuations at phase boundaries enhance lattice friction as dislocations cross those boundaries.
The enhanced lattice friction raises the activation energy for dislocation climb and glide.
Boundary-induced inhibition of dislocation climb and glide reduces creep strain rate relative to a single-phase or non-optimized dual-phase coating.
An optimized balance of FCC and BCC phases will yield lower creep strain rates than the stated baseline.
An optimized balance of FCC and BCC phases will yield longer creep lifetimes than the stated baseline.
The proposed mechanism is effective only over temperatures and stresses for which the dual-phase microstructure remains stable.
Temperatures that cause phase coarsening or interphase-boundary degradation can eliminate the proposed creep-resistance mechanism.
The magnitude of creep-resistance improvement depends on phase ratio, grain size, and operating temperature.
